readerTitle: Your best cleaner just became the boss. Should she keep cleaning?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 업체, B2B IT 지원 회사) + 실제 저서·연구 (Andy Grove, Linda Hill) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 관리자의 성과는 내가 직접 한 일이 아니라 팀 전체가 낸 결과다. 팀원 각자를 조금씩 낫게 만드는 일이 내 최고의 작업보다 더 큰 숫자가 된다.
misconception: 가장 일 잘하는 사람이 관리자가 되면, 계속 직접 일을 많이 할수록 팀에 도움이 된다.

sources.text: Grove, A. S. (1983). High Output Management. Random House. (관리자의 성과 = 자기 조직의 성과 + 영향을 미치는 주변 조직의 성과)
Hill, L. A. (1992). Becoming a Manager: Mastery of a New Identity. Harvard Business School Press.
청소 업체와 IT 지원 회사의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 청소 업체 계산: 선택 A = 마리아 6집 + 팀 6명 × 4집 = 30집. 선택 C = 마리아 2집 + 팀 6명 × 5집 = 32집. 팀원 1명당 +1집 × 6명 = +6집으로 마리아의 원래 주간 작업량(6집)과 같음. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.

Grove의 공식("A manager's output = the output of his organization + the output of the neighboring organizations under his influence")은 High Output Management에 나옵니다. 카드에는 직접 인용 대신 풀어 쓴 문장으로 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
Linda Hill의 연구는 신임 관리자들을 첫해 동안 추적한 연구로 알려져 있습니다(대상 인원은 약 19명으로 알려짐). 카드에는 인원 수를 쓰지 않고 일반적으로 서술했습니다. '신임 관리자들이 관리를 권한과 통제로 오해했다가 관계와 팀 성과로 다시 이해하게 된다'는 요약이 원문과 맞는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your best cleaner just became the boss. Should she keep cleaning?
body: Maria is the fastest, most careful cleaner at a home-cleaning company. She cleans 6 homes a week. Everyone else cleans 4.
So the owner makes her team lead over the other six cleaners. Her first instinct is to keep cleaning, because that's what she's great at. The numbers say something surprising about that instinct.

image.label: A cleaner holding a mop, now standing in front of a small team
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 청소 도구를 든 여성이 앞에 서 있고, 뒤에 같은 유니폼을 입은 청소원 여섯 명이 서 있음. 여성의 손에 든 대걸레가 반쯤 클립보드로 바뀌는 모습. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should Maria spend her first months as lead?
body: Maria now leads six cleaners who each clean about 4 homes a week. Some homes need a second visit because spots get missed. Schedules are messy.
What's the best use of her week?

options.text: Keep her full cleaning schedule and handle team issues after hours
options.feedback: Her 6 homes stay safe, but the team gets only her leftover, tired hours. The bigger number, the other 24 homes, doesn't move.

options.text: Stop cleaning entirely and manage from the office
options.feedback: She frees up time for the team, but loses her feel for the work and her credibility with cleaners. Stepping away completely can go too far, too fast.

options.text: Clean a couple of homes, and spend the rest training, checking work and fixing schedules
options.feedback: She gives up some of her own output to raise everyone else's. The next card shows why that trade pays.

cards.title: Count the whole team, not just Maria.
body: If Maria's training and better scheduling help each cleaner do just one more home a week, the team gains 6 homes. That equals her entire old output. She cleaned a third as much, and the team cleaned more.

breakdown.label: Option C: Maria leads the team
Gain from one extra home each
breakdown.detail: Same as Maria's whole week of cleaning

cards.title: From doer to manager
body: A **doer** is measured by their own work. A **manager** is measured by what their team produces.

Andy Grove, the former Intel CEO, put it plainly in *High Output Management* (1983): a manager's output is the output of the team they run, plus the teams they influence. Your own tasks still count, but only as one small part of that total.
So a manager's main question changes from "what should I do?" to "what will raise the team's results most?"

image.label: One tall bar versus six bars each growing a little
image.brief: 왼쪽에 높은 막대 하나("Your own work"), 오른쪽에 막대 여섯 개가 각각 조금씩 위로 자라는 모습("+1 each"). 오른쪽 막대들의 늘어난 부분을 합치면 왼쪽 막대와 같은 높이가 된다는 점을 점선으로 보여줌.

cards.softwareNote: A strong engineer promoted to lead faces the same math. Unblocking five engineers, reviewing their work and clearing up priorities usually adds more shipped work than the lead's own code.

cards.title: Doing feels productive. Managing often doesn't.
body: A cleaned home is visible by lunchtime. A training session shows results weeks later, in other people's work. Doers get quick, clear feedback. Managers mostly get slow, blurry feedback.

Harvard professor Linda Hill followed new managers through their first year for her book *Becoming a Manager* (1992). Many started out thinking the job was about authority and control. Over the year, most came to see it as building relationships and getting results through others. That shift took time and felt uncomfortable.

cards.title: The same trap, in every business.
list: **A head baker** who still shapes every loaf while new bakers guess at the recipe
**A sales manager** who closes the big deals personally, so no rep learns how
**A partner at a firm** who rewrites every report instead of showing staff what good looks like
cards.callout: In each case, the manager's own work looks great. The team's work stays where it was.

cards.title: Don't disappear from the work.
body: On small teams, the manager often has to keep doing real work. A two-person shop can't afford a full-time boss. The point is to choose that work on purpose, not by habit.
Staying close to the work also helps. Managers who never touch it lose their sense of what's hard, and their judgment about quality slips.
And the payoff isn't automatic. Time away from tasks only helps if it goes to things that actually lift the team, not to extra meetings.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: Dev was the best engineer at a company that runs IT systems for small businesses. He now leads five support engineers.
At 6 p.m., a key client's email server goes down. Dev knows he could fix it in an hour. What should he do?

options.text: Fix it himself tonight. The client matters too much
options.feedback: The client is happy tonight. But the next outage still needs Dev, and his team learns nothing.

options.text: Work through it with one engineer at the keyboard, then have them write up the fix
options.feedback: It may take longer tonight, but now two people can handle this problem, and the write-up helps the rest of the team.

options.text: Assign it to the on-call engineer and log off
options.feedback: It builds independence, but a high-stakes outage with no support can go badly for the client and the engineer.

cards.title: Your job is the team's output, not your own.
body: When you start managing, a small gain for each person usually beats your best individual work.
**Try it today:** list what you did last week. Mark each task: did it raise your own output or your team's? Pick one task to hand off or teach next week.
